item.research_question: Can a single-phase face-centered-cubic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy be fabricated via 3D ink-extrusion using inexpensive blended oxide nanopowders followed by co-reduction and sintering, and what are the resulting microstructural and mechanical properties?
item.material_system: Co3O4 + Cr2O3 + Fe2O3 + NiO blended oxide nanopowders (target composition: 25Co-25Cr-25Fe-25Ni at.%), poly-lactic-co-glycolic-acid binder, dibutyl phthalate plasticizer, ethylene glycol butyl ether surfactant
item.processing_route: 3D ink-extrusion printing of oxide-polymer ink using nozzles of 200–510 µm diameter; de-binding at 150 °C and 300 °C for 30 min each; co-reduction and sintering in flowing H2 (99.999%, 250 ml min−1) at 1557–1573 K for 1 h with heating rate of 10 K min−1
item.test_conditions: Tensile testing of single filaments (125 µm diameter, 10 mm gauge length) at 293 K and 130 K; compressive testing of micro-lattices (solid volume fractions 25–63%) at 77 K and 293 K; in situ synchrotron XRD in flowing H2 (1.3 ml min−1, 19.9 keV) from room temperature to 1215 K
key_findings: Final relative density achieved is 99.6 ± 0.1% after sintering at 1573 K for 1 h, with porosity of 0.4 ± 0.1%.
Strut diameters as low as 103 µm were produced using a 200 µm nozzle, demonstrating isotropic shrinkage of 78% in volume.
Tensile yield strength at 293 K is 250 ± 5 MPa with ultimate tensile strength of 598 ± 8 MPa and fracture strain of 33.8 ± 1.3%.
At 130 K, yield strength increases to 388 ± 7 MPa, ultimate tensile strength to 864 ± 12 MPa, and fracture strain to 37.6 ± 0.7%.
In situ XRD reveals sequential reduction: Co, Fe, and Ni form rapidly between 573–673 K, while Cr2O3 reduction begins above 1073 K.
Final microstructure consists of equiaxed grains sized 5 to 25 µm containing annealing twins.
Average coefficient of thermal expansion calculated as 21.6 ± 0.5 × 10–6 K−1 between 293 and 1215 K.
Micro-lattices show no catastrophic cracking up to 50% strain, with stress increasing continuously due to stretching-dominated plastic deformation.
item.mechanism: The process relies on the rapid sequential reduction of Co3O4, Fe2O3, and NiO to form metallic Co, Fe, and Ni, which initiate densification. Cr2O3 reduces slowly above 1073 K, and the resulting Cr diffuses into the Co-Fe-Ni matrix, forming a single-phase fcc CoCrFeNi alloy. The isotropic and homogeneous shrinkage during co-reduction and sintering preserves the printed architecture despite a 78% volume reduction, while the small initial agglomerate size (<10 µm) and high surface area enable fast reaction kinetics and near-full density.
item.limitations: Residual sub-micrometer porosity and swelling voids remain after sintering; the measured yield stress is lower than bulk values due to the small number of grains (2–3) across the filament diameter; larger unreduced Cr2O3 particles can act as diffusion barriers and sintering inhibitors, leading to local encapsulation.
item.future_work: Hot isostatic pressing could be applied to eliminate residual closed porosity; the method allows for compositional flexibility to create compositionally-graded HEAs or combinatorial alloy discovery; the technique can be scaled for high-volume production of lightweight, high-ductility structures operating from liquid nitrogen up to ~1000 °C; miniaturization to sub-micron scale lattices could push mechanical performance limits.
quotes: A complex phase evolution path is observed by in-situ X-ray diffraction in extruded filaments when the oxide phases undergo reduction and the resulting metals inter-diffuse, ultimately forming face-centered-cubic equiatomic CoCrFeNi alloy.
The final mass loss after holding under H2 for 1 h at 1557 K is measured at 28.3%, in good agreement with the theoretical value of 27.5%.

At 130 K, the yield stress, ultimate tensile strength and fracture strain are all increased to 388 ± 7 MPa, 864 ± 12 MPa, and 37.6 ± 0.7%, respectively, demonstrating the outstanding combination of strength and ductility of CoCrFeNi at cryogenic temperatures.
